Standard MC implementations often generate more than one triangle per cell, making iso-splatting significantly more storage-efficient [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that 'Iso-splatting generates one point per cell (n vertices), while triangle-soup MC generates 3n vertices; iso-splatting is more storage-efficient.' This directly supports the claim that standard MC implementations generate more than one triangle (specifically, up to 3 vertices/triangles depending on interpretation, but the text contrasts 1 point vs 3n vertices) per cell, making iso-splatting more storage-efficient.
unsupported
Quadrilateral splats are efficient as they can be implemented by passing a single vertex to graphics hardware [S1].

The claim states that quadrilateral splats are efficient because they can be implemented by passing a 'single vertex' to graphics hardware. However, the evidence (Source [S1]) explicitly states that for surface splatting, each sample must be characterized by 'location, normal, and a local variance matrix'. It further specifies that 'each point sample consist of sample location, function value, gradient, and a local variance matrix.' Therefore, the implementation requires passing multiple data attributes (location, normal, variance matrix, etc.), not just a single vertex. While the method uses point primitives (which might be interpreted as vertices in a geometric sense), the data payload is complex, contradicting the simplicity implied by 'passing a single vertex' as the primary efficiency mechanism described in the claim.

# Step 4: Project to isosurface [S1]

The claim describes the 'iso-splatting' method detailed in Source [S1]. The evidence confirms that it is a point-based alternative to isosurface visualization (Abstract, Intro), generates point samples per cell (Section 4), and projects them onto the isosurface using function values and gradients (Section 3, Eq 5-6). The displacement threshold formula (∆d = 0.5 * sqrt(sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2)) is explicitly stated in the text. The Newton-Raphson approximation for t and the projected point p'λ are derived in the text. The handling of local maxima/minima by discarding points exceeding ∆d is mentioned. The point sample data structure (location, function value, gradient, variance matrix) is described. The cell subdivision criterion based on function value interval width is noted. The comparison of storage efficiency (1 point vs 3 vertices for MC) and performance (half extraction time, quadruple framerate) is supported by the text. The implementation using QSplat-style splatting is mentioned. The claim accurately reflects the facts presented in the source.
supported

-   One point per cell may miss fine details or multiple components within a cell [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that 'a given cell may contain several disjoint components of the same isosurface' but the method 'generates a point sample' (singular) per cell. It further notes that 'Often, the contribution to the isosurface of a given cell can be approximated cheaply without sacrificing overall rendering quality,' implying that generating only one point per cell is an approximation that may miss details (such as multiple disjoint components) when the cell contains complex geometry.
